extra_misconceptions.fact: Rubbing frostbitten skin with snow or hands ruptures intracellular ice crystals and causes permanent tissue damage.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Vigorous rubbing with snow is an effective field method to restore circulation to frostbitten fingers and toes.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Up to eighty percent of ultraviolet radiation penetrates cloud cover and reflects off snow, requiring UV-blocking goggles.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cloudy winter days on the mountain eliminate the risk of ultraviolet corneal burns known as snow blindness.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cold air and altitude blunt the thirst reflex while respiratory moisture loss increases, requiring scheduled water intake.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Thirst is a reliable early warning indicator for dehydration during cold, high-altitude winter sports activities.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cessation of shivering in a cold patient signals progression from mild to severe hypothermia, requiring urgent evacuation.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A skier who stops shivering in subfreezing wind is warming up and adjusting well to the cold mountain environment.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to core body temperature if you rub frostbitten extremities or rewarm tissue near a direct campfire?
Which physical indicator distinguishes mild hypothermia with active shivering from severe hypothermia on a cold slope?
What measurement of wind speed and ambient air temperature confirms when exposed skin will freeze in under thirty minutes?
Why is it dangerous to wear non-UV-rated dark lenses at high altitude when bright sunlight reflects off fresh snowfields?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Warning markers must be planted firmly uphill in full view of traffic above any blind roll so riders have room to stop.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Placing crossed skis immediately beside an injured downhill skier provides sufficient warning time for approaching riders.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A rigid ski boot acts as an effective anatomic splint, and Ski Patrol has specialized tools to remove it safely indoors.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Removing a tight ski boot immediately after an ankle or lower leg crash reduces swelling and prevents tissue injury.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Unless an immediate hazard threatens life, keep the injured rider still to protect the spine and shield them from traffic.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Moving an injured snowboarder off the trail to the trees is always the first step before contacting Ski Patrol.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Accurate dispatch requires the exact trail name, nearest lift tower number, trail intersection, and injury description.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Reporting only the general mountain peak name gives Ski Patrol enough location detail to locate a downed skier.

extra_socratic_questions: Where should a Scout position crossed skis or a snowboard above an injured skier to warn oncoming downhill traffic?
Which specific location markers on a lift tower or trail map allow Ski Patrol to dispatch a rescue toboggan fastest?
Why is it dangerous to remove a crashed skier's helmet or unbuckle their boots when spinal trauma is suspected?
Under what condition does an uninsulated casualty lying directly on packed snow lose body heat faster than in cold air?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Trail ratings are relative only to trails within that specific resort, meaning a blue run at one mountain may match a black elsewhere.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Trail difficulty symbols represent absolute pitch angles that are standardized identically across every ski resort worldwide.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Each trail rating pairs a distinct geometric shape with its color so skiers can identify difficulty regardless of color vision.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Trail rating signs use only color to communicate difficulty, so colorblind skiers cannot distinguish trail ratings.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Changing weather, afternoon shade, and heavy skier traffic can turn a groomed beginner trail icy or bumpy within hours.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A trail marked with a Green Circle remains guaranteed free of ice patches, moguls, or low-visibility hazards all day.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An orange oval marks a terrain park containing man-made jumps, boxes, and rails that require advanced aerial control.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: An orange oval trail marker indicates a slow-speed family learning zone reserved for first-time downhill skiers.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to expect a Blue Square trail at a steep rocky resort to match a Blue Square on a small local hill?
Which symbol and color designate a freestyle terrain park containing jumps, rails, halfpipes, and man-made features?
What slope gradient and grooming characteristics distinguish a Green Circle run from an ungroomed Black Diamond chute?
Under what weather or snow surface condition can a groomed Green Circle trail ski like a much harder intermediate slope?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Sustained isometric muscle contractions at high altitude demand strong aerobic and anaerobic endurance to prevent fatigue.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Downhill skiing relies on gravity to pull the skier down the slope, so cardiovascular endurance is unnecessary.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Core stability, hip mobility, and lower-body eccentric leg strength drive edge control and balance across all snow sports.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Upper body bicep strength is the primary physical attribute required to turn skis or control a snowboard on steep terrain.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Injury rates peak late in the afternoon when muscle fatigue slows reaction times and compromises joint stabilization.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Most recreational ski and snowboard knee injuries happen on the very first run of the morning before muscles warm up.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Ballistic bouncing in cold muscles triggers the stretch reflex and causes micro-tears; use dynamic movements to warm up first.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Bouncing aggressively at the end of a cold toe-touch stretch before boarding the chairlift prevents muscle pulls.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to knee ligament stability during a late-afternoon run when quadriceps and hamstring endurance is depleted?
Which muscle groups absorb eccentric braking forces when carving turns down a steep mogul field or choppy snowpack?
What measurement of recovery heart rate or timed wall-sit stamina tracks readiness for a full day of alpine skiing?
Why is it dangerous to perform cold static hamstring stretches at the summit instead of a dynamic warm-up before skiing?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Doubling socks compresses foot blood vessels, restricts warm blood circulation, and causes faster cooling and blisters.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Wearing two thick pairs of wool socks inside a ski boot doubles foot warmth and prevents frostbite in subzero weather.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A single heavy coat traps sweat without ventilation flexibility, whereas a three-layer system allows moisture management.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A heavy one-piece insulated parka over a cotton t-shirt is warmer and safer than three thin, separate clothing layers.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Snow pant cuffs and gaiters belong over the outside of the boot shell; tucking fabric inside creates painful pressure points.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Tucking heavy waterproof snow pants inside the top cuff of a ski boot keeps snow out and improves lower leg control.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Thick hats with pom-poms alter helmet geometry and cause the shell to shift on impact; use only a thin helmet liner.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A winter knit beanie worn underneath a ski helmet improves impact absorption and keeps the helmet secure on the head.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to convective and conductive heat loss when sweat saturates a cotton sweatshirt during a cold chairlift ride?
Which physical indicator during a helmet fit check confirms the chin strap and brow gap will protect you in an impact?
Under what exertion and weather condition should you open pit zips or shed a fleece mid-layer before climbing a slope?
Why is it dangerous to wear two thick pairs of socks inside a fitted ski boot or snowboard boot on a subzero day?

extra_misconceptions.fact: People ahead or downhill always have the right-of-way because they do not have eyes in the back of their heads to see uphill.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A downhill skier who makes wide, unpredictable turns across the slope must yield the right-of-way to faster riders above.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Landing zones are blind spots from the takeoff lip; riders must clear the landing area immediately after every jump or fall.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sitting down on the snow directly beneath the lip of a terrain park jump is a safe spot to rest out of the wind.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Vocal warnings do not override the uphill skier's duty to maintain control and leave ample space when passing anyone ahead.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Calling out "on your left" transfers the legal responsibility for avoiding a collision to the slower skier ahead of you.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Closed trails may harbor avalanche blasting, winch cables, or thin snow cover, and entering them violates the safety code.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Ducking under a boundary rope onto a closed trail is permissible if fresh powder covers the rocks and no groomers are active.

extra_socratic_questions: Which skier or rider holds the right-of-way when a faster expert approaches a slower beginner weaving across the trail?
What step in the SMART Style progression requires inspecting a terrain park jump's takeoff and landing before hitting it?
Where should a Scout position themselves when stopping on a narrow trail to check a map or wait for patrol buddies?
Why is it dangerous to ride a snowboard without a leash or ski without working retention brakes on an icy slope?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Leaning back unweights the ski tips, where steering edges engage, causing the skis to accelerate uncontrollably downhill.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaning backward toward the tails of the skis helps a downhill skier slow down and maintain control on steeper slopes.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Over-tightened bindings fail to release during a twisting fall, transferring excessive torque directly to knee ligaments.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cranking ski binding release settings to the maximum number prevents all falls and protects the knees from twisting.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Pole straps must be removed before loading the chairlift so a snagged pole cannot pull the skier back into the moving chair.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Keeping ski pole straps wrapped tightly around the wrists while riding a chairlift prevents dropping poles in deep snow.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Turning both skis across the fall line so the uphill edges bite into the slope is the proper technique to shed speed and stop.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pointing skis straight down the fall line is the safest way for a beginner to stop when gaining too much speed on a hill.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to edge grip and turn initiation if an alpine skier leans backward into the backseat on a steep icy pitch?
What measurement of skier weight, height, age, boot sole length, and ability determines an alpine binding DIN release setting?
Which physical indicator on a slope shows the exact direction of the fall line before you initiate linked parallel turns?
Why is it dangerous to leave chairlift safety bars raised or keep ski pole straps wrapped around your wrists on the lift?
